rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a second
why: "for a second" is used as a generic duration marker for an unrelated moment (puzzling over a license plate), exactly the universal-timer crutch the rule bans
suggestion: including one that took her a few seconds of squinting to place

rule_name: Hedge Where the Character Could Not Know, Cut Filler Everywhere Else
quote: just so many of them
why: "just" is filler softening a claim the narrator is entitled to make plainly; the character could simply state the fact
suggestion: There are so many of them.

rule_name: Emotional Detachment, Render the Physical Correlate, Not the Label
quote: Her stomach drops, her hands go cold
why: "stomach drops" and "cold hands" are named verbatim in the rule as the banned physiological clichés that could describe any anxious character
suggestion: The backs of her knees go loose, her fingers won't close all the way

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for about a second
why: another instance of the universal "for a second" duration filler, applied to a flashback moment with no real timed specificity
suggestion: for three full steps she isn't in the hallway at all

rule_name: Reification and the grep test
quote: everything she's holding comes loose at once
why: an unanchored abstraction ("everything") is given the physical verb "holding" as if her composure were an object she was gripping
suggestion: Her jaw unclenches and her shoulders come down all at once.

rule_name: Emotional Detachment, Render the Physical Correlate, Not the Label
quote: Chloe's hands are still cold
why: a second use of the banned "cold hands" cliché from the rule's own example list, carrying no specificity to this character or moment
suggestion: Chloe's fingers still won't make a full fist when she sits down.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a second
why: a third occurrence of the same generic "for a second" duration filler, now attached to a different character and a different kind of moment
suggestion: He turns the six over, weighing it against the seven and a half.

rule_name: Ration a Character's Verbal Tic to the Moments It Characterises
quote: for a second
why: the same timed-duration habit that marks Chloe's anxious moments elsewhere in the chapter is reused here for Sam with no characterizing purpose, reading as narrator autopilot rather than a signal tied to one character
suggestion: He turns the six over, tilting his head at it.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: He thinks he's funny
why: states the interiority of a non-POV character directly, matching the automatic-fail table's own example ("Sam thinks about it longer than he wants to") almost exactly
suggestion: Sam grins at his own joke before anyone else does, half the time.

rule_name: Joining speech and body
quote: "Pluto." Chloe is doing her shoes
why: a period splits one continuous beat (answering while not looking up) into two sentences where the rule calls for a comma splice to keep it one moment
suggestion: "Pluto," Chloe says, still doing her shoes, not looking up.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: nobody has ever talked at her before
why: an absolute claim about Chloe's whole life functions as a narrator superlative ("never...before"), the category the automatic-fail table cuts on sight
suggestion: Chloe doesn't mind. She keeps both hands still in her lap and lets it run.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: which was worse
why: an unattributed narrator ranking of the mother's comment against the daughter's, matching the banned "narrator evaluation / ranking" pattern
suggestion: and what the girl's mother said about it afterward

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: which means she was already dressed
why: a "which" clause that tells the reader how to interpret the six-minute fact instead of letting it stand, the exact shape of the banned evaluation clause
suggestion: her mom is at the front desk in about six minutes, already dressed, hair not brushed

rule_name: The trailing clause
quote: rather than anywhere she'd have to settle into
why: the sentence is complete at "by the window"; the tail exists only to tell the reader how to read the mother's posture, the trailing clause the rule cuts
suggestion: Her mom is still in her shoes, sitting on the arm of the chair by the window.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: Chloe stops hearing the words and hears only that it's still going
why: routes the moment through the perception verb "hears" twice instead of rendering what the drifted-out sound is actually like
suggestion: Somewhere in the middle of it the words blur into one long hum, still going.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: which is the wrong thing to say to a parent at seven in the morning
why: a narrator ranking clause telling the reader how to judge Chloe's line, the same shape as the table's banned "which is the good part"
suggestion: "Since before I was born," Chloe says. Her mom laughs at it anyway.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: which takes about a second
why: a fourth reuse of the generic "a second" timer, here as a throwaway trailing clause rather than a real detail
suggestion: She tells him the name of it. He says nothing back.

rule_name: Vague Abstractions, Replace "Something," "Nothing," "The Whole Thing"
quote: Chloe has something to say about the pool
why: "something" stands in for an actual, nameable thought that the reader never gets, the exact gray placeholder the rule targets
suggestion: Chloe has a whole sentence about the lid ready.

rule_name: Thought Reported vs. Thought Rendered
quote: She works out about how long it would take to say and doesn't say it
why: states that a calculation happened instead of rendering it, a summary of thinking rather than an instance of it
suggestion: She counts the words she'd need—four, five—and lets them go.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: because she's due back at work
why: an obvious causal clause explaining a fact the reader can already infer, the pattern the automatic-fail table cuts
suggestion: She leaves on the Sunday.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: Chloe knows what he's doing
why: routes the observation through the banned filter verb "knows" instead of rendering the recognizable behavior itself
suggestion: Chloe recognizes it: the four correct words, then nothing.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: always correctly
why: an absolute modifier in narration functions as the same kind of superlative claim ("never once", "the only time") the table cuts on sight
suggestion: He answers when he's called on, in about four words.

rule_name: Inhabit the Subject, and Give the Reader One Line of It
quote: And it's mostly the gas that does it anyway, not the heat, which is why some of them go straight up in a column and some of them just pour out the side and go down the road at walking speed.
why: Kavi's volcano explanation runs to a full paragraph of subject content across two turns; the rule caps a student's technical content at one line before returning to the person
suggestion: Cut to: "It's the gas that does it, not the heat." Move the column-versus-lava-flow detail into action or Chloe's observation instead of more of Kavi's dialogue.

rule_name: Banned Constructions, Assert Nothing, Show the Substance
quote: you're right, I said that wrong
why: "you're right" is in the explicit banned family and "I said that wrong" is a close variant of banned "I was wrong"; the verdict is asserted instead of shown
suggestion: "Mass." He wipes the word out and writes the other one into the gap it leaves.

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction, Don't Normalise by Reporting an Absent Reaction
quote: Nobody says the word interrupting, and nobody says the word attitude.
why: reports an absent reaction from the whole class as proof that Ruth's outburst was treated as unremarkable, instead of showing one specific reaction
suggestion: One kid glances at Ruth and looks back at the board. Nobody else looks up.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: Nobody says the word interrupting, and nobody says the word attitude.
why: two stacked negative clauses joined by "and", the exact shape of the banned "Nobody makes an announcement, nobody says anything at breakfast" example
suggestion: The class moves on like nothing was said.

rule_name: Emotional Detachment, Render the Physical Correlate, Not the Label
quote: Chloe sits there with her heart going.
why: this is verbatim the rule's own banned example of a physiological cliché that carries no specificity
suggestion: Chloe presses her thumbnail into the edge of the desk until it leaves a mark.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions
quote: She watches Mr. Doyle's face the next time Ruth's name comes up. She watches at the door on the way out, in case somebody's waiting there to have a word.
why: the frame verb "watches" is repeated four times across this passage (for it, Mr. Doyle's face, the door, the lunch table), the exact repeated-frame-verb failure the table names
suggestion: She watches for it the whole rest of the period—Mr. Doyle's face, the door on the way out, the far end of the lunch table.

rule_name: Thought Reported vs. Thought Rendered
quote: She thinks about it that night and still doesn't know what to do with it
why: summarizes the fact of thinking rather than rendering the thought's own rhythm or interruption
suggestion: That night it snags—Ruth said it, nothing happened, so—and she still doesn't put her hand up.

rule_name: Dialogue Tag Clutter, Let Action Beats Carry Tone
quote: Priya says it without looking up from the drawer she's pushing shut with her knee
why: loads the tag with a prepositional explanation of circumstance instead of splitting the physical beat into its own sentence
suggestion: Priya doesn't look up from the drawer, pushing it shut with her knee. "Do you ride?"

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
quote: You're agreeing at me.
why: the four-turn exchange from Ruth's line through this one carries only a single tag, forcing the reader to count lines to track who's speaking, the same shape as the rule's own four-line example
suggestion: "You're agreeing at me," Sam says, not looking up from his tray.
